claims.text: Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how strongly the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its own price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: PED is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: PED is stated as an absolute value: the negative sign that the law of demand produces is dropped by convention, so PED is compared with 1 without the sign.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand is price-elastic when its PED value is greater than 1: quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price changed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand is price-inelastic when its PED value lies between 0 and 1: quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price changed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The responsiveness shown by a demand curve is read from its slope in relation to the axes: a curve drawn steeply against the price axis suggests a given price change moves quantity demanded little, while a flatter curve suggests quantity demanded moves far for the same price change.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The whole quantity range matters when classifying elasticity: the same demand curve can hold a stretch where demand is elastic and another where it is inelastic.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: On a demand curve drawn as a straight line, demand tends to be elastic at high prices and small quantities and inelastic at low prices and large quantities.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: In a demand diagram, elasticity is seen by comparing how far the point moves along the quantity axis against how far it moves along the price axis.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The main determinants of PED are the availability and closeness of substitute goods, the proportion of income the purchase takes, whether the good is a necessity or a luxury, the width of the market defined, and the length of time since the price changed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand for a good with close substitutes that are easy to switch to tends to be price-elastic, because a price rise pushes buyers towards the substitute.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand for a good that takes a small share of a consumer's income tends to be price-inelastic, because even a sizeable percentage price rise changes the household budget little.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand for a necessity tends to be price-inelastic, while demand for a luxury tends to be price-elastic, because a necessity is bought even at a higher price while a luxury can be postponed or dropped.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A narrowly defined market tends to have more elastic demand than a widely defined one, because a narrow market is the one whose substitutes sit next door.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand tends to become more responsive to a price change as the time since the change lengthens, because habits, contracts and information adjust slowly.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: What the elasticity figure measures is sometimes confused with what makes it that size: the calculation of PED is arithmetic on two percentage changes, while the determinants are the features of the product and its market that explain the figure.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Total spending by consumers on a good, which equals the seller's revenue from it, is calculated as the price multiplied by the quantity sold.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where demand is price-inelastic, a price rise tends to raise total spending on the good, because quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rose.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where demand is price-elastic, a price rise tends to lower total spending on the good, because quantity demanded falls by a larger percentage than the price rose; the mirror rule, that a price rise raises spending, holds only where demand is price-inelastic.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: In a demand diagram, total spending at a price is read as the rectangle drawn from the origin to that point on the demand curve: its height is the price and its base is the quantity demanded, so a price movement changes spending according to how the rectangle's area responds.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Revenue and profit are different quantities: revenue is all the money coming in from sales, while profit is what remains after the costs of production are paid, so a revenue change alone settles nothing about profit.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Spending on one product is not the same as total demand in an economy: the elasticity in this topic is the responsiveness of buyers of one good, examined one market at a time.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Comparing a total with an average is a different calculation: total spending is price times quantity over the whole market, while an average figure divides a total by a count, and the two must not be exchanged.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A producer deciding the price of its product is likely to weigh PED because the effect of a price change on its revenue depends on whether demand for the product is elastic or inelastic.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A government choosing an indirect tax is likely to weigh PED, because a tax tends to raise more revenue where demand is price-inelastic, since quantity demanded falls little when the tax pushes the price up.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where a government wants a tax to change behaviour rather than to raise money, it is likely to pick goods whose demand is price-elastic, because the quantity bought responds to the price rise the tax causes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: PED is usually estimated from past market data, so decisions that lean on it carry the risk that the elasticity measured yesterday drifts as substitutes, incomes and tastes change.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Price elasticity of demand is sometimes confused with price elasticity of supply: the demand version measures how buyers respond to a price change, while the supply version, taught in topic 2.8, measures how sellers respond.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand is perfectly inelastic when PED equals 0: quantity demanded does not change when the price changes, so the demand curve is drawn as a vertical line.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand is perfectly elastic when PED is infinite: at one price buyers take any quantity offered, while at any higher price quantity demanded falls to zero, so the demand curve is drawn as a horizontal line.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Demand has unit elasticity when PED equals 1: the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, and the demand curve is drawn as a curve bending towards the origin along which price multiplied by quantity is the same at every point.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where demand is price-elastic, a price cut tends to raise total spending, because quantity demanded rises by a larger percentage than the price fell; where demand is price-inelastic, a price cut tends to lower total spending, because quantity demanded rises by a smaller percentage than the price fell.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where demand has unit elasticity, a price change leaves total spending unchanged, because the change in quantity demanded offsets the change in price; on the diagram the spending rectangles before and after the change have the same area.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: For consumers, PED signals how a price change will hit their budgets: where demand for a good is price-inelastic, a price rise tends to raise what they spend on it and squeeze spending on other goods, bearing hardest on low-income households, while where demand is price-elastic they can protect their budgets by switching to substitutes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
